newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-D.Babcock cuts jobs in break even bid.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-D.Babcock cuts jobs in break even bid.

text.p: Embattled German plant engineering group Deutsche Babcock AG plans massive job cuts under a restructuring aimed at wiping out losses by 1997-98, new chairman Klaus Lederer said on Tuesday.

The reorganisation could force the company, which builds power plants, airports and machinery, to cut as many as 10,000 jobs -- a third of the present workforce -- partly through sales of subsidiaries.
Deutsche Babcock aims to simplify its operations radically, cutting the number of group companies to 100 from the current 286, Lederer told the annual news conference.
"I believe we have a chance to rebuild this company," said Lederer, who took up the post this month. He was formerly chief executive of ITT Automotive Europe GmbH.
Lederer took over from Heyo Schmiedeknecht, who led an acquisition spree that ended up dragging the group deep into the red and straining bank credit lines.
Deutsche Babcock, which had a pretax loss of 400 million marks ($235 million) in 1995-96, aims to halve that loss this business year, and eliminate it entirely next year.
That may still leave it in a precarious position. A further loss of 200 million marks this year would nearly exhaust its remaining paid-in capital of 268 million marks.
But finance director Fritz Kall said the company had a 600 million mark credit line from banks to finance its restructuring, of which it has not touched a pfennig.
Investors reacted favourably to the restructuring news, with Babcock shares rising six marks to 76.50 marks in afternoon trade on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange.
The company said it saw incoming orders rising to 9.6 billion marks in 1996-97 and 10.3 billion marks the following year from 8.4 billion last year.
Sales are expected to rise to 9.6 billion marks this year and 9.9 billion next year from 8.7 billion last year.
In the first four months of the current year, which started on October 1, Deutsche Babcock reduced its loss to 150 million marks from 250 million in the year-earlier period.
Group incoming orders in the four months were unchanged at 2.8 billion marks, with order books flat at 11.4 billion. Turnover was up to 1.9 billion marks from 1.8 billion.
The workforce was down 13 percent to 29,303.
The company plans to invest 150 million marks both this year and next, down from 195 million marks in the year just ended. It plans to expand its business primarily in Asia and Latin America.
The company said subsidiaries accounting for 70 percent of its sales were profitable last year.

Of the remaining loss-making units, it plans to sell companies accounting for 13 percent of sales, and restructure others accounting for 17 percent of sales. It may also sell some profitable units to raise cash, Lederer said.

Earlier plans called for Babcock to reduce its workforce to 28,500 this year and 28,000 next year from 32,300 at the end of the 1995-96 business year. But Lederer said his first two weeks on the job have showed him that more would be necessary. A great many management-level jobs would be affected, he warned.

Up for sale will be DB Handel, Baldwin Steel, Flender ATB, Flender AAT, EMG and others Lederer declined to name. The company will decide within the next few weeks whether to sell Schumag, for which it has unsuccessfully sought a buyer since last summer, Lederer said.
The company has enlisted the help of Boston Consulting Group and Droege & Co. in planning its restructuring.
-- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097150 $ = 1.703 German Marks)
